summary: This article explains why the light, small ball in table tennis makes it one of the fastest reaction-time sports, and how spin and paddle angle control its path.
introduce: Draw a simple cause → effect arrow on the board and ask students for an everyday example, such as “I did not sleep, so I felt tired.” Tell them that while reading “Table Tennis: Fast Reflexes” they will find at least two cause-and-effect links.

keyTerms.def: how quickly a person responds to something that happens
a fast turning movement given to an object
the direction or slant at which something moves or meets something else

challengeTerms.def: the speed of something in a certain direction
a turning movement around a center point
a very fast, automatic response to something

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that reaction time matters more than strength in most sports? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain how two different science ideas from the article help a player win a rally.
struggling: Read the first part of the article aloud together, review reaction, spin, and angle, and let weak readers match cause cards to effect cards from the article with a partner.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses velocity, rotation, and reflex to explain one important cause-and-effect chain from the article.
